question: What are the three main types of names used to identify a medication?
explanation: You'll see drugs referred to by their chemical name (the atomic blueprint), generic name (the official name), or brand name (what the company calls it to sell it). Great job keeping these straight! [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why do nurses avoid using chemical names of drugs during routine clinical practice?

options.A: Chemical names change every time a new company manufactures the drug
options.B: Chemical names are strictly reserved for pharmacy dispensing staff only
options.C: Chemical names are too complex and difficult to use safely in daily care
options.D: Chemical names only describe the inactive filler ingredients in the tablet

explanation: Chemical names are full of complex molecular descriptions. Imagine trying to read one out quickly during an emergency ward round—way too tricky! That's why we stick to generic and brand names. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h1)

question: What is the primary characteristic of a generic drug name?

options.A: It is exclusively owned and trademarked by one manufacturing company
options.B: It is the official non-proprietary name for the active ingredient
options.C: It changes depending on which country the medication is imported from
options.D: It describes the exact atomic arrangement of the chemical structure

explanation: The generic name is the universal, public name given to the active drug, no matter who manufactures it. Think of it as the drug's true identity! [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h2)

question: How do drug name stems help a student nurse understand unfamiliar medications?

options.A: They show the exact expiration date and proper storage temperature needed
options.B: They tell the nurse the exact retail price of the medication in the pharmacy
options.C: Common suffixes reveal the pharmacological class and general action of the drug
options.D: They indicate which manufacturing company produced the specific batch of pills

explanation: Drug stems (like '-olol' for beta-blockers) are like cheat codes! They tell you what family a drug belongs to, helping you guess its action even if you've never seen it before. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h2)

question: What is another common term used to describe a brand name drug?
explanation: A brand name is also called a proprietary name because the company 'properly' owns the rights to that specific marketing title. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h3)

question: Why might a single generic drug molecule have multiple different brand names on the market?

options.A: Generic molecules automatically mutate into different brand substances over time
options.B: The government requires the drug to change its name every five years
options.C: Hospitals rename the drugs to avoid confusion with local herbal remedies
options.D: Different manufacturing companies create their own unique trademarked names for marketing

explanation: Different pharmaceutical companies want their version to stand out, so they create catchy brand names for the exact same active medicine. Paracetamol is a great local example of this! [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h3)

question: Which component must be identical in both generic and brand name drugs?

options.A: The retail price in the pharmacy

explanation: Regulatory bodies ensure that whether you buy the expensive brand name or the affordable generic, the active healing ingredient inside is 100% the same. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why are generic drugs generally much more affordable than brand name drugs?

options.A: The government subsidizes all generic manufacturing costs in local factories
options.B: Generic medications are manufactured in smaller quantities than brand drugs
options.C: Generic drugs use lower quality active chemicals to reduce production expenses
options.D: Makers of generic drugs do not carry the original research and marketing costs

explanation: Developing a new drug takes billions in research and advertising. Generic makers skip those initial costs, which is why their prices are much friendlier to patients' pockets. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h4)

question: Which agency is primarily responsible for regulating medications in Nigeria?
explanation: NAFDAC is our national watchdog ensuring that every drug distributed in Nigeria is safe and genuine. You'll see their stamp on almost every medication package! [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of regulatory oversight on generic and brand drugs in the country?

options.A: To ensure medications are safe, effective, and free from harmful counterfeits
options.B: To eliminate the need for nurses to check patient identification bands
options.C: To prevent foreign countries from exporting medical supplies to local hospitals
options.D: To make sure all pharmaceutical companies charge the exact same price

explanation: Agencies like NAFDAC protect the public by cracking down on fake or expired drugs, ensuring patients get real healing when they take their medications. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h5)

question: Why must a nurse know both the generic and brand names of a medication?

options.A: To ensure the hospital charges the patient the highest possible fee
options.B: To prevent medication errors during charting and prescription checks
options.C: To help patients manufacture their own medicines at home safely
options.D: To comply with legal rules requiring nurses to write prescriptions

explanation: Knowing both names protects your patient. If a doctor writes a brand name and the chart has the generic, you'll instantly spot it and prevent accidental double-dosing! [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h6)

question: A doctor prescribes a brand name drug for a patient, but the hospital dispenses the generic equivalent. What is the most appropriate action for the nurse?

options.A: Administer the medication, knowing the active ingredient is identical
options.B: Discard the medication because generic drugs cannot be substituted safely
options.C: Call the doctor to report that the pharmacy gave an unauthorized fake drug
options.D: Refuse to give the drug until the brand name version is brought from home

explanation: As long as the active ingredient and strength match, the generic drug is therapeutically equivalent and totally safe to give your patient. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h6)

question: What should a nurse tell a patient who is worried because their new generic refill looks different from their old brand name pill?

options.A: Confirm that the pharmacy made a dangerous mistake and gave them the wrong chemical
options.B: Explain that physical appearance changes can happen, but the active medicine inside is the same
options.C: Advise the patient to crush the pills and mix them with water to test their strength
options.D: Tell the patient to stop taking the medication immediately and return it to the manufacturer

explanation: It's normal for patients to panic when a pill changes color or shape. Reassure them that different makers use different inactive dyes, but the active medicine doing the work is identical. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended practice when educating patients about safe medication use?

options.A: Asking a healthcare provider when unsure about a medication change
options.B: Purchasing medicines exclusively from licensed and verified retail pharmacies
options.C: Buying prescription drugs from informal open-air street markets for lower prices
options.D: Checking prescription labels carefully to understand both generic and brand names

explanation: Never encourage buying drugs from street hawkers or open markets! Always guide patients to licensed pharmacies to avoid fake or degraded medications. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h7)
